## 131. Updating both halves: there is no route, and that is the design (added 2026-10-14)

The owner asked for this directly, on 2026-10-14: one Update control that
updates both the desktop program and the Python backend. **This section exists
to say that it added nothing to this API**, so a reader looking for the routes
of that feature finds the reason instead of nothing.

The backend half runs `scripts/apply-patches.ps1` *on the PC*, from the desktop
app, over the repository it was cloned into. That is a filesystem operation
against the folder Jarvis runs from, and there is deliberately no route for it:

- a phone cannot run it (the script, the repository and the Python folder are
  all on the PC, and the work is `git apply`, then `pip`, then the test suites);
- a route would put "replace the files this PC runs" behind the pairing token,
  reachable from anywhere on the owner's private network. That is a new way in,
  and this project's rule 4 is that nothing acts without the person at the
  machine.

So `tools/check_parity.py` has nothing to classify here, and
`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries the one-sided row that says why the phone is
not offered a control that could not work. The desktop's own half of the
feature — the signed release check — added no route either; it is
`jarvis-desktop/src-tauri/src/update.rs`, unchanged in what it requests.

`docs/ONE-UPDATE-FOR-BOTH.md` is the whole design: the order (backend first,
executable second, and the executable not at all when the first half did not
finish), where the app reads the two paths from, what the owner configures once,
and the three questions deliberately left for the owner.


## 132. Action receipts, and one button to put a change back (added 2026-10-14)

`backend/jarvis_receipts.py`, its drop-in folder `plugins/ready/receipts/`,
and the goals tick wired to it. The idea is borrowed from
BasedHardware/omi: an action that CHANGES something leaves a receipt saying
what changed, with one button to put it back.

### 132.1 What was missing

Every other record in this backend says what Jarvis was ALLOWED to do
(`approvals.db`, `jarvis_gate.py`) or what was SAID (`chat-history.db`).
Nothing said what an action actually changed - so an action that was allowed,
ran, and turned out to be wrong left no way back except doing the opposite by
hand, from memory. `jarvis_inbox_tidy.py` and `jarvis_forget_range.py` each
keep an Undo of their own, in memory, for ten minutes; neither records
anything another module could read. `jarvis_sources.py` is a "tool receipt"
of a different kind: what an ANSWER read, read-only.

### 132.2 The store

One table, `action_receipts`, in its own SQLite file beside `goals.db` and
`schedule.db` - `receipts.db` in the settings folder, `JARVIS_RECEIPTS_DB`
overriding it - opened once per call, closed by the caller, WAL, a 10-second
busy timeout, exactly as `jarvis_chat_log.py` and `jarvis_gate.py` do it.
**Deliberately not a table in `approvals.db`:** that file is one of the nine
`jarvis_gate.py` refuses to let any tool modify, because the approval stamp
lives in it, and receipts are written by the same call path as the action they
record - which would hand every recorded action a write path into the file
the gate trusts.

| column | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `receipt_id` | `"rc"` + 12 hex characters (`uuid4`, like every other id here) |
| `created_at` | when the change was made |
| `tool_name` | which action changed it (`"goals.mark_step"`) |
| `summary` | what changed, in the owner's own words, scrubbed |
| `before_snapshot_json` | enough to put it back, scrubbed, capped at 8,000 characters |
| `after_snapshot_json` | what it looks like now, scrubbed |
| `undo_callable` | the code that can put it back, BY NAME (`"jarvis_goals.restore_row"`) |
| `undone_at` | when Undo really ran, or NULL |

`receipts.db` joined the locked backup on 2026-10-14 (`jarvis_backup.SOURCE_DBS`,
with every other database): a receipt holds the owner's own words - what
changed, and what the thing looked like before - so a restore that put
`goals.db` or `projects.db` back while dropping the receipts for those rows
would leave Undo pointing at changes the archive had already replaced. The
archive is encrypted before it touches a disk, so those words are never in the
clear.

### 132.3 The four functions

```
record(tool_name, summary, *, before=None, after=None, undo=None) -> str
undo(receipt_id) -> dict
recent(limit=20) -> list
get(receipt_id) -> dict | None
register_restorer(tool_name, fn)     the code that applies a before snapshot
```

`record()` is called BEFORE the change: the before snapshot is what Undo
writes back. It **never raises into the caller** - a receipt that cannot be
written returns `""` and is audit-logged by name only, because a receipt must
never fail the action it was recording.

**Nothing unscrubbed is ever written.** `jarvis_scrub.scrub_text` cleans the
summary and every string in both snapshots, keys included, so a key, token or
password that happened to be in the words an action changed lands as
`[redacted: ...]`. With no scrubber at all, `record()` returns `""` and writes
nothing - the same rule chat history follows with no key. A snapshot larger
than the cap is replaced by a note saying so rather than truncated, and Undo
reads that note as "not enough to restore" and refuses rather than putting
back half of a row.

### 132.4 Undo is idempotent, and says which way it went

The claim is one conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE receipt_id=? AND undone_at IS
NULL`, run BEFORE the reversal: only the caller whose UPDATE changed a row
reverses anything, so a double tap, two screens or a retry cannot apply the
reversal twice. A second call is refused in plain words - *"this was already
undone"* - and `undone_at` is set only when the reversal really ran. If the
reversal itself fails, the claim is released and the reason returned, so a
receipt is never left marked undone when nothing was put back. The one honest
gap: a process killed between the claim and the reversal leaves it marked
undone, and it will not be applied again.

Two ways back, and the answer says which one ran:

1. **`"path": "callable"`** - the zero-argument callable `record(undo=...)`
   was given, still held in this process. It is the exact code that made the
   change, so it is preferred.
2. **`"path": "snapshot"`** - a new process has no in-memory callable, which
   is the normal case rather than an error. The store takes the restorer
   registered for that `tool_name`, or resolves the name in the row
   (`undo_callable`) in its own module, importing it when it is a `jarvis_`
   module and not already loaded - which is what runs its `register_restorer()`
   again - and calls it with the parsed before snapshot.
3. **Neither** - it refuses, in plain words, and leaves `undone_at` NULL so it
   can be tried again.

### 132.5 The two routes

```
GET  /api/receipts                       the recent list, newest first
     ?limit=<n>                          whole number, 1 to 200 (default 20)
POST /api/receipts/<receipt_id>/undo      put one change back
```

Both are installed by the module's own `install()`, wrapped round the core's
Handler after its own origin and token checks, exactly as `jarvis_news.py`,
`jarvis_sources.py` and `jarvis_goals.py` do it. **No patch is involved:**
`plugins/ready/receipts/plugin.json` names `jarvis_receipts` with
`"install": "handler"`, and `jarvis_plugins.py` makes the call the patch would
have made. `stack_order` is 149 - after every folder the old patch stack had
(the highest is `model-lanes` at 146).

The list answers `{"ok", "receipts", "count", "limit", "undo_action",
"undo_tier", "waiting", "last", "words"}`. Each receipt carries its own
`"undoable"` flag, worked out in this process, so an app is never offered a
button that can only refuse. `"last"` is how the most recent Undo card ended,
in fixed plain words from the module's own table - never a payload.

**A locked view withholds the whole list (Q1, 2026-10-20).** `GET /api/receipts`
also accepts `?app_locked=1` / `?hide_memory_lists=1`. When either is set - or
the one trusted hook, `jarvis_private_view`, says so - the answer is
`{"ok": true, "withheld": true, "private": true, "why": "...", "receipts": [],
"count": 0, ...}` with the honest sentence (`"Hidden while App lock is on."` or
`"Hidden while \"Hide memory lists and chat history\" is on."`), and `recent()`
is never called, so no summary or path leaves the database. The flags can only
ADD withholding: `0`, `false`, an unknown spelling or a `force_unlock` key
changes nothing, and no request can clear the trusted state. The live HUD must
eventually pass the state; until it does, the apps keep hiding the drawer
themselves.

**Undo is a mutating action, so it goes through the ONE permission model**
(ARCHITECTURE §3): ONE card, action `undo_action`, and the reversal runs only
on the gate's own answer. A denied or timed-out card changes nothing at all,
and at tier `ask` only an outcome of `"approved"` counts as a yes - `allowed`
alone is not "a human decided", because the gate returns `allowed=True` at
tier `notify` and at tier `auto` with nobody in the loop. The receipt id is
checked, and the receipt's own state read, BEFORE any card - no card is ever
raised for a receipt that cannot be undone, and a receipt already undone is a
plain 409 with no card. One card at a time, like every other card in this
project. The route answers 202 and the reversal runs on its own thread: a card
can wait fifteen minutes and an HTTP request must not.

**Which tier, and why the module does not decide it.** The shipped
`jarvis-framework.toml` gives `undo_action` a line of its own: **"ask"**, one
card per undo, which is what this feature is for. Until 2026-10-16 it had none
and took `unknown_action_tier`, which that file also says is "ask", so the card
is the same one either way and the line only pins it. It was added because a
fall-through is invisible - `backend/test_gate_names.py` reports a name with no
line anywhere as an action the running gate cannot resolve - and because which
card this raises should not depend on a setting that can be loosened. The
module does **not** force the tier, and that is deliberate rather than an
omission. `jarvis_gate.py` carries
`_NO_RULE_FROM_DENIAL`, the list of actions whose always-ask, button-started
"no" must not become a proposed standing rule; `backend/test_gate_denial_rule.py`
reads every module that refuses to act on any tier but `ask` and requires its
action to be on that list. Joining it means editing `jarvis_gate.py` - one of
the files this feature is forbidden to touch, and a patch is the thing the
drop-in folder exists to avoid - so this module takes the tier the gate gives
it, exactly as `jarvis_media.py` and `jarvis_news.py` do, and the tier table
stays the single policy with one reader. The consequence, said plainly: if the
owner writes a different tier for `undo_action` in their own settings file, his
file is what the gate reads - "ask" is the shipped default, and it is the value
this action already had.

**`undo_action` is deliberately not in `jarvis_gate.py`'s `_RISK` table**, and
this feature adds no row for it: a row means patching the gate, and the
drop-in folder exists so a new route needs no patch. An action nobody
classified is treated by the gate's own fail-closed rule as irreversible and
outbound, which makes the Undo card risky (Windows Hello on the PC, the screen
lock on the phone) and heavy. That is stricter than the action it undoes,
which is the safe direction to be wrong in - and it is said here so a reader
does not think the card was classified on purpose.

### 132.6 What is wired to it today

**One mutation, on purpose and named:** `jarvis_goals.Goals.mark_step` - the
everyday tick, no card, one tap, often by voice, and the easiest change in
this backend to make by accident. A receipt is written before the row changes,
holding the whole row (`plan`, `status`, `changed`, `checkin_job`), the tick
result carries `"receipt_id"` (null when the receipt could not be written),
and Undo puts the plan back EXACTLY - the same `done_at`, the step that waited
on it locked again - rather than re-ticking or clearing it. `restore_row()` in
`jarvis_goals.py` is the restorer, registered at import, so the snapshot path
works after a restart. `jarvis_goals.py` imports `jarvis_receipts` lazily,
inside a `try`, in both places: a backend folder without the module still
ticks steps.

Not wired, and said plainly: goals `create`/`accept`/`stop`, everything in
`jarvis_projects.py`, and every other mutating module. Each needs its own
honest reversal - deleting the row a draft created, putting back the check-in
job `delete` removed - and inventing one that does not truly reverse the
change is worse than not offering the button.

### 132.7 Neither app has a screen for it yet

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries the row: the machine-readable half is built
and both routes are live, and the UI is not built on either app. When it is,
it goes on BOTH, on this same store and this same card. `tools/check_parity.py`
now carries both routes in its `BACKEND_ONLY` register (2026-10-28), with that
follow-up written in the reason, so the gap is named rather than invisible.
## 133. "Write Like Me": drafting in the owner's own voice (added 2026-10-15)

**Drafting-turn wiring (Q4 follow-up, 2026-10-20).** `jarvis_agent.run_local_turn`
puts the owner's own (stripped) style examples in front of a LOCAL DRAFTING turn
only: `jarvis_voiceprint.drafting_request()` recognises "draft / write / reply /
rewrite / in my voice" requests, `infer_register()` picks one of the five
registers, and `drafting_block()` returns the rules + examples only when the
feature is on, at least one sample exists, the turn is not Temporary and it is
not an external-chatbot path. A non-empty block is inserted as a data system
message before the answer and latches the turn local (`latch_taint`, why
`voiceprint_exemplars`); the empty/off/temporary/external path returns "" and
does NOT latch. No lane, tools list, card or route changes.


**Slice 1 hardening (Area 5 / 2026-10-20).** The stripping step now replaces a
name that OPENS a sentence too, by four rules: a possessive (`Priya's` -> `[name]`),
a direct-address vocative (`Sam,` / `Hi Sam,` -> `[name],`), an honorific
(`Dr. Patel` -> `[name]`), and a name repeated at the start of two sentences.
Closed sets keep `It's ready.`, `Thanks, I'll check.` and ordinary conversational
openers intact; the no-digit guarantee is unchanged. `score_style_compliance`
now flags a draft that copied a stripping placeholder (`[name]`, `[number]`,
`[amount]`, `[date]`, `[link]`, `[email]`, `[path]`, `[handle]`, `[postcode]`,
`[time]`) as `leaked_placeholder: true` with score 0, and `add()` strips
chat-control markers (`<|im_start|>`, `<|im_end|>`, `<|endoftext|>`,
`<tool_call>`, `<think>`) before the scrubber and the store.

**Slice 1b hardening (2026-10-20, final audit Part I).** `exemplars()` now reads
the owner's OWN saved samples from `voiceprint_samples` in `voiceprint.db`
(lexical overlap with the question, each text through `strip_entities`, and the
memory store only as the supplement when fewer than `k` matches), so a
calibration sample or edited draft is no longer invisible to `prompt_block()`.
`add()` itself refuses a secret through `_secret_in()` before the scrubber and
the store, so a direct Python caller cannot bypass the route's check. And every
mutating POST (`sample`, `learn_edit`, `forget`) is **this PC only**:
`_from_this_pc()` uses `jarvis_owner_check.from_this_pc`, failing closed, with
loopback-only as the fallback when the helper is absent. GET stays the existing
token-guarded read. This PR adds **no** `enabled` route: PR #665 owns it.

**Scope note.** The plugin already mounts `GET /api/voiceprint` and three POSTs
through `jarvis_voiceprint.install()` (origin + token); no new route or HUD
patch is added here. `prompt_block`/`drafting_block` IS mounted into a local
drafting turn now, at the turn-loop seam this note used to name:
`jarvis_agent.run_local_turn` inserts the block before the answer - see the Q4
paragraph at the top of this section, which supersedes the earlier BLOCKED note
here (2026-10-20). `voiceprint.db` is already in
`jarvis_backup.SOURCE_DBS`; a global Forget hook is also BLOCKED (no safe
per-database hook in `jarvis_forget_range.py`).

**V2 UI slice (2026-10-20; PR #665, wired).** The desktop page
(`jarvis-desktop/src/voiceprint-settings.js`) and its Rust bridge
(`src-tauri/src/voiceprint.rs`: status/add/forget/set-enabled, every request
bounded to 30 s, no proxy, no redirects), and the phone's `net/WriteLikeMe.kt` +
`ui/screens/VoiceprintPlate.kt`, are now MOUNTED on both apps, in the same
place and under the same words: the "How Jarvis talks" card. Desktop: the empty
`<section id="voiceprint">` in `settings.html` is drawn by
`voiceprint-settings.js`, mounted once from `manner-settings.js`; the four
commands are registered in `lib.rs` + `build.rs`, with a generated permission
each and the `voiceprint` set in `permissions/surfaces.toml`, granted to the
Settings window only (`capabilities/settings.json`). Phone: the same card, under
`MannerSection` (`MannerPlate.kt`), through `JarvisApi`/`JarvisRuntime`.

A read is never held; the three writes (the switch, "Keep this sample", "Forget
this sample") are held while the event stream is stale - in the page, in Rust
(`look::stale`, the same `STALE_HELD` sentence every other Settings write uses)
and on the phone (`actionBlocker`). The page and the phone read the answer the
PC really sends: `GET /api/voiceprint` returns
`{"ok", "samples": [...], "count", "voiceprint", "status": {...}}`, so the
switch, `available` and `scrubber` are read from `status`, while the samples and
the count are top-level (measured against `handle_get` on 2026-10-20). The
ON/OFF switch is `POST /api/voiceprint/enabled {"enabled": bool}` (the earlier
draft's `"on"` is accepted as an alias) - a local setting
written to `voiceprint.json` beside the other settings, with no card, no model
and no network; absent means the framework's own `[voiceprint] enabled` value.
Forget asks "are you sure?" first on both clients, and one tap is one change.
No approval card is raised anywhere: these are local settings.

Who may send what (2026-10-20 audit, catch 2C; owner's decision the same day):
adding or forgetting a sample is **this PC only** - `install()` refuses
`sample`/`learn_edit`/`forget` from another device before the body is read,
because the sample text is the owner's own words. The local ON/OFF switch is
deliberately **exempt** from that guard: it carries none of the owner's words,
it is an ordinary client setting like "How Jarvis talks", and the paired
phone's switch has to keep working - turning it off is instant, and neither
direction raises a card. `backend/test_voiceprint.py` pins both halves.

`backend/jarvis_voiceprint.py`, and its drop-in folder
`plugins/ready/voiceprint/`. Four routes, no patch, its own store.

### 133.1 What this is

Jarvis writes prose as the owner: email drafts, notes, messages. This engine
makes those drafts sound like him, in three steps that are all plain code on
this PC - find how he has written about something similar before, take the
names and numbers out of that example, and measure the result against a
**voiceprint**: a small set of numbers worked out from his own writing.
Nothing is sent anywhere, no weights are changed, and the model is shown
examples at generation time, which is the one approach that fits on this
hardware and can be undone.

### 133.2 Why this is not `jarvis_style.py`

There was already an earlier version of steps one and two in
`jarvis-backend/jarvis_style.py`. It is **delivered to nobody**: measured with
`python -B tools/check_unmanaged_files.py`, the file is classified **NEITHER** -
no patch the installer applies writes it and `$SHIPPED` does not carry it - and
the repository holds exactly one copy of it. An edit there reaches no PC. The
owner's decision (2026-10-15) was to build the engine in a new module and leave
that file untouched, rather than promote it into `$SHIPPED`, which would make
`apply-patches.ps1` start overwriting a file it has never managed, on every run.
`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries the full reasoning and the limitation that
comes with it. `jarvis_voiceprint` deliberately never imports `jarvis_style`,
and does not name it in a string either; its suite asserts both.

### 133.3 The store

`voiceprint.db`, in the same settings folder as `goals.db` and `schedule.db`
(`JARVIS_VOICEPRINT_DB` overrides the file, for the tests). One connection per
call, `with closing(...)`, WAL and a busy timeout - the pattern
`jarvis_receipts.py` uses. One table:

    voiceprint_samples (id, created_at, kind, prompt, text, numbers)

`kind` is `calibration`, `edit` or `sample`. `numbers` is the voiceprint worked
out from that one sample.

### 133.4 Every write is guarded, and fails closed

The pattern is `jarvis_receipts.py`'s, copied on purpose: its `_scrubber()` at
`jarvis_receipts.py:289-295` ("Fails CLOSED: no scrubber, nothing recorded")
and its refusal at `:443-449`. Here, `_scrubber()` returning `None` means
`add()` returns `""` and the store is **not even created**. Text is scrubbed
BEFORE it is stored, so nothing unscrubbed is ever on disk to be listed later.
A sample that looks like it holds a password, a key or a one-time code is
refused (`jarvis_scrub.find_secret`), not stored, and the refusal says so in
plain words.

### 133.5 The four routes

    GET  /api/voiceprint                    the samples, the voiceprint numbers
                                            and what the engine is doing. A read.
    POST /api/voiceprint/sample             {"text": "...", "prompt"?: "..."}
    POST /api/voiceprint/learn_edit         {"before": "...", "after": "...",
                                             "prompt"?: "..."}
    POST /api/voiceprint/forget             {"id": "vp...", "confirm": true}

All four go through the server's own origin and token checks, the same as every
other route. They arrive with no patch: `plugins/ready/voiceprint/plugin.json`
names the module and `jarvis_plugins.py` makes the call the patch would have
made.

### 133.6 The permission model, said plainly

`sample` and `learn_edit` write the owner's OWN words into a store on his OWN
PC, and raise **no approval card**. That matches the owner's decision of
2026-09-24: facts learned from his own words are saved without a per-fact yes.
It is a memory write, not an action on the world, and nothing leaves the PC -
retrieval goes through `jarvis_memory`, so it trips the same taint latch every
other memory read trips and the turn stays on the local model.

`forget` is deliberately harder. The owner kept the question (2026-09-24: every
learned thing is listed with a Forget that "asks 'are you sure?' first ...
because forgetting cannot be undone"), so the route **refuses** a forget whose
body does not carry `"confirm": true`, with `"needs": "confirm"` and a sentence
saying why. That is the question, enforced in the one place a different client
cannot skip it. A missing id and an already-forgotten id are both refused
rather than treated as success.

### 133.7 What it strips, and the guarantee

`strip_entities` carries the earlier engine's eight regular expressions and its
proper-noun walk, and closes the gaps a read-only probe measured: `_DATE` now
runs before `_PATH` (a slash-date used to leave its day behind as
`14[path]`), `_PHONE` accepts a leading `0` (a UK area code used to survive),
and times, postcodes, decimals and grouped numbers are caught. It ends with a
pass that replaces any remaining run of digits, so **no digit survives** - the
invariant is a property of the code, and `backend/test_voiceprint.py` asserts
it for every row of the module's docstring table and for every line of that
docstring. One limitation is named in §8 rather than hidden: a name that OPENS
a sentence is not replaced.

### 133.8 Neither app has a screen for it yet

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries the row. The store and the four routes are
built; the Write Like Me card calls `/api/voiceprint`, `sample` and `forget`
from BOTH apps (PR #665), and `learn_edit` has no app surface yet - when it is
built BOTH apps get it, and the `BACKEND_ONLY` register (2026-10-28) names it.
## 134. The blind credential vault: a NAME everywhere, the value at the point of use (added 2026-10-14)

**The idea, in one line.** The model, the prompt, the approval card, the audit
line, the event payload and every returned string carry an opaque handle -
`{{vault:github}}` - and the real value is put in **once**, on the one line that
builds the outbound request that authenticates with it. Anything that comes back
is run through `jarvis_scrub` before it is returned, so a service that echoes the
key back cannot leak it. `backend/jarvis_vault.py`; borrowed from Meta's Muse and
from the blind-credential-handle idea generally.

**Where the value lives.** Windows Credential Manager, through
`jarvis_token_store.WindowsStore` - the same store, the same generic-credential
format and the same three ctypes calls the pairing token and the Exa/Tavily/Brave/DeepSeek
keys already use, one entry per name under `Jarvis Backend/vault/<name>`. This
section adds no second mechanism to keep in step with the old one. **Values are
never written to any file**: `<config folder>/vault.json` holds the names, the
host each is bound to and when each was last used, and running the suite searches
those bytes for the value, a prefix of it and its length. With no Credential
Manager there is no fallback to plain text - `put()` refuses and `status()` says
why.

**The two routes** (drop-in: `plugins/ready/vault/plugin.json` names the module
and the loader calls its `install()`; no patch, no core change):

| route | what it answers |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/vault/handles` | every name, its handle, the host it is bound to, when it was last used and whether a value is really there - **never a value, never a masked prefix of one, never a length** |
| `POST /api/vault/put` | `{"name", "value", "for_host"}` - store one secret. ONE approval card at tier `ask` |

**The card, and what a denial does.** `POST /api/vault/put` is a mutating action,
so it goes through the one permission model: `jarvis_gate.check()` under the
action `vault_put`, tier `ask`, with the card's words written in the module and
never assembled from the request. A denied, timed-out or refused card returns
`403`/`503` with "nothing was stored" and **nothing is stored** - and nothing is
stored *before* the answer either: `put()` is not reached until the card has been
decided, and the suite reads the store from inside the gate itself to prove it. A
verdict of `allowed=True` is not enough: the tier must BE `ask` and the outcome
must be `approved` (`allowed=True` also comes back on tier `notify` with nobody
asked - ARCHITECTURE §3, "`allowed` is not 'a human decided'"). A gate that
cannot be reached fails closed. The value is never echoed back, in the answer or
in a refusal.

**`resolve()` is the one place a value is substituted**, and it is bounded:
`{{vault:name}}` is replaced exactly once per occurrence; a handle that names
nothing, or a value the store will not hand over, is left as the literal handle
(a visible placeholder beats an empty string that authenticates wrong); and a
handle **bound to a host resolves only for that host**. Rule 3's "sent only to the
one service it authenticates against" is therefore a property of this function
rather than of every caller remembering it: with no host given, a bound handle
does not resolve at all.

**The one real use, and why that one.** `jarvis_search.py` builds the credential
header for the Exa, Tavily, Brave and DeepSeek keys from the provider's own handle, and
`_send()` substitutes it. Those three keys are the right first call site because
each goes to exactly ONE host that is fixed in code (`api.exa.ai`,
`api.tavily.com`, `api.search.brave.com`) - so the host binding can be enforced
rather than trusted - and because a web search is "one request, one key, one
service" with nothing in between. An empty vault changes nothing at all: the key
is still read from the Credential Manager entry it always was. A provider that
echoes the key into its answer is cleaned on the way back, both by putting this
turn's values behind their handles and by the project's scrubber.

**Deliberately not wired, and why.** `jarvis_browser_control.run()` has taken a
`secrets(name, host)` hook since `browser-engine.patch`, and `jarvis_agent`'s
`_run_browser_control` has never passed one - so a `<secret>` step stops today
with "no secret store was given to this run". The vault is *not* plugged in there:
a browsing turn can be pointed at any site, and a store that hands a value to
whatever host the page is on would break rule 3's "only the one service it
authenticates against" in exactly the place it matters most. Wiring it belongs
with a per-site binding the owner chooses, which is a decision, not a plumbing
job.

**The tests that bite.** `backend/test_vault.py` (196 checks) searches the
returned JSON, the audit details, `handles()`, `status()` and `vault.json`'s own
bytes for the value - and for a masked prefix and the length - rather than
asserting a flag; proves a four-character value is still hidden though the
scrubber's own exact-match floor is eight; proves a denied card writes neither the
store nor the file; and runs a real server on 127.0.0.1 to prove end to end that
the vault's key reaches its one service, that a key bound elsewhere is not sent,
and that the service's own echo of the key does not come back in the result.

**Backend only, on purpose, and this is the whole reason.** Neither app has a
vault screen and neither calls these two routes: a value is typed on the PC, in a
setting or through `POST /api/vault/put` from this machine, and the phone is
never asked for one - the same rule the web-search keys already follow
("Keys are entered on the PC only ... the phone never asks for one: sending a key
to the PC would send it somewhere other than its own service",
`jarvis_search.KEY_ENTRY`). A phone screen for this would be a screen whose whole
job is to carry a secret over the network to a machine that can read it from its
own Credential Manager, which is more exposure for no gain.
`GET /api/vault/handles` carries no value, so it is safe for an app to read; the
desktop and phone halves are simply not built yet, and `tools/check_parity.py`
reports both routes as the backend's own until one is.

## 135. The skill library's other doors: four routes under `/api/skills/hub` (added 2026-10-15)

`backend/jarvis_skill_hub.py`, and its drop-in folder `plugins/ready/skill-hub/`.
Four routes, no patch. **It adds no route that already existed**: the list
(`GET /api/skills`) and the removal (`POST /api/skills/decide`, with the "are
you sure?" before it) are in §6's tables and stay exactly where they are. This
section documents the four routes that are new, and nothing else.

### 135.1 What this is

A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` in it, and `jarvis_skills.py` owns
everything about one: the frontmatter parser, the scanner that refuses the
attack patterns the OpenClaw marketplaces really used, the quarantine, the
~100-token card, the full body, installing, removing and writing. This module
**re-implements none of that and calls all of it.** It adds the four things
that were missing around it:

1. **the reference manuals.** `parse_skill` already walked a skill's folder and
   recorded every file in it, `references/<file>.md` included, in the skill's own
   file list; nothing in the backend ever read one. A manual is now listed by
   name and size for free, and read only when a caller asks for that one - which
   is what keeps a large manual at zero tokens until it is wanted;
2. **leading `/skill` and `/bundle` commands.** Up to five tokens off the FRONT
   of a message, stopping dead at the first one that is not a known skill or
   bundle, so `/path/to/file` is never swallowed;
3. **a project's own skills**, at `<project folder>/.jarvis/skills`, for
   projects the owner explicitly trusted;
4. **`/learn`**: a four-section distillation (When to Use / Procedure /
   Pitfalls / Verification), scrubbed, and saved only through
   `jarvis_skills.write_skill()`.

### 135.2 The four routes

```
GET  /api/skills/hub/references?skill=<name>            the manuals a skill ships
GET  /api/skills/hub/references?skill=<name>&file=<ref>.md
                                                        ONE manual, read now
GET  /api/skills/hub/projects                           a trusted project's skills
POST /api/skills/chain         {"text": "/skill-a /bundle rest of the message"}
POST /api/skills/learn         {"topic", "steps"|"procedure", "when",
                                "pitfalls", "verification", "name"}
```

All four are installed by the module's own `install()`, wrapped round the
core's Handler after its own origin and token checks, exactly as
`jarvis_receipts.py` (§132.5) does it. **No patch is involved:**
`plugins/ready/skill-hub/plugin.json` names `jarvis_skill_hub` with
`"install": "handler"`, and `jarvis_plugins.py` makes the call the patch would
have made. `stack_order` is 147 - after every folder the old patch stack had
(the highest of those is `model-lanes` at 146).

The first route answers twice, on the same path, and the two forms report
failure differently - one HTTP status, one payload - which a client has to know.
With `?skill=` alone it lists: `{"ok", "name", "references": [{"reference",
"bytes", "too_big_to_read"}], "note"}` - names and sizes, and **no text of any
kind**. A missing `?skill=` is a 400; a skill that does not parse, or that is not
there, is a 404. With `&file=` it reads that one manual and the answer is
**always 200**, carrying `{"ok", "name", "reference", "text", "bytes",
"findings", "warnings", "note"}` - a refusal is `{"ok": false, "refused": true,
"findings": [...]}` **with no `text` key at all**, so a client that only checks
the status code is told `ok` and must read the body. A manual is one `.md` file
name inside the skill's own `references/` folder: a separator, a `..`, an
absolute path, a name that is not there, or anything over 256 KB is refused with
its reason rather than opened.

The second route answers `{"ok", "skills", "quarantined", "skipped", "dirs"}`
for every skill under every trusted project's `.jarvis/skills`. "Trusted" is
not a second opinion invented here - it is `jarvis_projects.check_folder()`,
the one check "Folders Jarvis may look in" already uses, asked again at use
time because a folder can be taken off that list after a project was made. A
project whose folder is no longer trusted is not looked in at all. 503 when
`jarvis_skills.py` or `jarvis_projects.py` is not on this PC, which is a real
answer rather than an empty list.

The third answers `{"ok", "skills", "missing", "rest", "stopped_because"}` -
the skill NAMES a chain asks for, the rest of the message untouched, and why
the chain stopped. It cannot run a skill, reach a skill's body, or read a
manual: it reads the index and returns names.

The fourth is the only route here that writes anything.

### 135.3 The permission model, said plainly

The three reads raise **no approval card**, which is what the gate's own table
already says: `skill_list`, `skill_load` and `skill_scan` are tier `auto`
(`jarvis_gate.py:850`). Reading a skill, listing its manuals, looking in a
trusted project's folder and parsing a chain are all things the owner can
already do by opening the folder.

`/api/skills/learn` is the writer, and **it reaches the write only through
`jarvis_skills.write_skill()`**, which is the existing scanner and the existing
card in the order that matters: it scans the body, refuses outright on a
`block` finding, and raises ONE `modify_own_code` card **before** it writes
(`jarvis_skills.py:799`, `:806`, `:816`). `modify_own_code` is `ask` in the
shipped `jarvis-framework.toml` (:281), so it is ONE card and it waits for a
person - the action does not exist unattended. Its risk row is
`("hard", "local")` (`jarvis_gate.py:278`), and measured against the gate's own
`risk_for()` that is `{"reversible": "hard", "reach": "local", "swipe_ok":
false, "why": "revertible from a backup, not from here"}`: **`swipe_ok` is
false**, so a gesture cannot approve it - the card has to be opened. **No new
gate row was needed and none was added:** the vocabulary already had
`skill_install` and `skill_write` mapped to `modify_own_code`
(`jarvis_gate.py:852-853`).

One thing is re-checked rather than assumed. `write_skill()` tests
`Verdict.allowed`, and `allowed` is `True` on the tiers `notify` and `auto`
where nobody was asked - `jarvis_skills.refine()` says exactly that about the
gate it shares (`:853-864`). So `learn()` reads the TIER itself and refuses
unless `modify_own_code` is `ask`, the way `jarvis_skill_discovery.offer()`
does. A settings file that listed it as `notify` cannot turn this card into a
rubber stamp.

### 135.4 A reference manual is scanned before it is handed over

A manual is text an agent will read and follow, exactly like a `SKILL.md`, so
it earns the same scanner. It is read and then passed through
`jarvis_skills.scan_text()` **before** it can reach a model: a `block` finding
returns `{"ok": false, "refused": true, "findings": [...]}` and **no text at
all**. A scanner that raises is a refusal too, not a pass - "the scanner did not
answer" and "the scanner said no" end in the same place.

The same rule covers a project's own skills, where it matters more: an
untrusted-looking skill in the owner's own project folder is parsed, scanned,
and **quarantined** if it fails - copied into `jarvis_skills.QUARANTINE` with
the reason written beside it (`jarvis_skills.py:621`) - and never loaded. **The
original is not deleted.** A skill that merely fails to parse is `skipped` with
the reason, not quarantined, because nothing was scanned to refuse.

**Added 2026-10-20 (Area 8B):** before the scan and before anything is
returned, the manual's text goes through
`jarvis_agent.strip_chat_markers` - the recursive SecAlign-style strip every
built-in tool result gets - so a chat-template instruction
(`<|im_start|>...<|im_end|>`) is removed rather than blended into a manual. A
reference name is one `.md` file name inside the skill's own `references/`
folder: `..`, `/`, `\` and absolute paths are refused, and the resolved parent
must be `<skill_dir>/references/`, so a symlink inside `references/` that
points out of the skill is refused too (`backend/test_skill_hub.py`, "a
reference is marker-stripped and a symlink cannot escape").

### 135.5 What it deliberately does not do

- **It does not re-document `GET /api/skills` or `POST /api/skills/decide`.**
  Both already existed, on both apps, with a caller; this feature touches
  neither and does not describe them again (§6).
- **It does not install a skill from anywhere.** There is no download, no
  import and no "install this skill" route: the only path to a new skill file
  is `/learn` → `write_skill()` → scanner → card → write.
- **It never deletes anything.** The one destructive-looking action is the
  quarantine, and that only copies.
- **It has no "yes to all".** No loop here raises a card, and there is no
  approve-all anywhere in the module - `backend/test_skill_hub.py` asserts both
  against the source with the comments stripped.
- **It reads no web page, email, document or note.** `/learn` writes down what
  its caller hands it and nothing else.
- **A project's skills are not leading `/` tokens.** Parsing a message must
  cost one small JSON read and must never run the scanner, so a project's own
  skills are reached through the projects route and their project, not by a
  bare command.

### 135.6 Neither app has a screen for it yet

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries the row. The four routes are live and neither
app calls any of them: no screen reads a reference manual, offers `/skill`
completion, lists a project's skills, or offers `/learn`. When they are built
they go on BOTH, on these same routes and this same `modify_own_code` card.
`tools/check_parity.py` carries all four in `BACKEND_ONLY` (2026-10-28), with
this follow-up in each reason, so the gap is named rather than read as a clean
pass it did not earn.

## 136. The cost advisor: no route at all, and it decides nothing (added 2026-10-14)

`backend/jarvis_auto_router.py`, and its drop-in folder
`plugins/ready/auto-router/`.

**This section exists to say that the feature added nothing to this API.** The
same shape as §131, and for the same reason: a reader who goes looking for the
routes of "the thing that decides whether a turn goes to the cloud" should find
the reason there are none instead of finding nothing.

### 136.1 The one sentence

**This module ADVISES. `jarvis_router.choose()` DECIDES.**

`choose()` (`backend/rebuilt/jarvis_router.py:590`) is the single authority on
which lane answers a turn. Its gates run in a fixed order and every one of them
can only move the answer *downward*, toward local - its own docstring says so
(`jarvis_router.py:596-600`: "the order is the policy ... none of them can
escalate past a gate that already refused"). `evaluate_route()` is a second
opinion about COST, never a second permission. It asks `choose()` directly
(through `_router_allows()`, with `owner_said_yes=True`), and any gate
`choose()` refuses on becomes its answer too, so it is **strictly weaker** than
the authority it advises about and can never open a gate that authority keeps
shut. A parallel gate stack in this position would be the failure
`jarvis_router.py:632-648` describes: a privacy decision with two sources of
truth, and so a gate nobody can see.

### 136.2 It serves no route, on purpose

`plugins/ready/auto-router/plugin.json` sets `install: "none"`, so
`jarvis_plugins.py` imports the module, calls `install()` **with no
arguments**, and prints its one banner line - *"advises on cost only;
jarvis_router.choose() still decides (no route)"*. No route is added, nothing
about a live turn changes, and there is therefore no `tools/check_parity.py`
row owed: a backend module with no route is outside what that tool decides.

That is deliberate: nothing new is reachable, so there is no new permission
surface to review, and the module cannot be hooked into a chat turn by
accident. Adding a caller is a separate change with its own review.

Owed anyway, and why: the callable below is a **frozen cross-module contract** -
Project Mode step 4 is written against this signature - and a contract another
module is built on is worth recording even when no HTTP call carries it. The
folder's own `README.md` says no *route* entry is owed, and that stays true;
this section records the *callable*, not a route.

### 136.3 The frozen contract

```
evaluate_route(prompt, context_tokens=0, active_project=None, speed_stats=None,
               *, last_turn=None, enabled=None) -> dict
```

**Never raises. Any input, including `None`, gives a dict.** Every key a caller
may act on:

| key | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `lane` | `"local"` or `"jarvis-escalate"` (a second name, `jarvis-critic`, went on 2026-10-27 - section 145.1) |
| `recommended` | `True` only when `lane` is a cloud lane |
| `advisory` | always `True` - this is advice, never a permission |
| `gate` / `reason` | which rule decided; `"cost"` when advice was given |
| `why` | the same thing in plain words, ready to show the owner |
| `est_local_seconds` | the estimated wait on this PC (an estimate, deliberately crude) |
| `complexity_score` | this module's own 0.0-1.0 score - **not** `jarvis_router.complexity()` |
| `category` | the work setup `jarvis_work.match()` found, or `"general"` |
| `tokens_per_s` / `tokens_per_s_why` | the rate used, and whether it was measured |
| `would_send` | the **scrubbed** text - empty unless gate 4 passed |
| `lane_if_allowed` | the lane that was under consideration |
| `thresholds` / `gates` | the two thresholds, and which of the gates passed |

A `recommended: True` result **always** carries a non-empty `would_send`, and
that is the only text the advice covers. The raw `prompt` is never handed back
as something to send: a caller that sends unscrubbed text has ignored this
function rather than been misled by it.

### 136.4 The four gates, then the cost question

The gates are inputs to the ADVICE. `choose()` remains the decision.

1. **Mode/switch** - OFF by default. On only when a caller passes
   `enabled=True` for this call, or inside an active Project Mode workspace
   whose `auto_route_cloud` is exactly `true`. A missing, unreadable, corrupt
   or non-object switch file (`auto-route.json`, beside the framework config)
   reads as **OFF** - the same answer for every one of those, because a switch
   nobody can read has not been turned on by anybody.
2. **Taint latch** - a HARD BLOCK, `reason="taint_latched_local_only"`. It
   reads the ONE latch this project has (`jarvis_gate.taint_active()`) plus a
   project whose `shareable` flag is not on, and not being able to read the
   latch also blocks. The honest limitation, named rather than rounded off:
   there is **one global latch, not one per topic** - `latch_taint()`'s `why`
   argument is a label nothing reads back - so ANY active taint blocks,
   whatever latched it.
3. **Budget** - two separate caps, because the project has two and they answer
   different questions: the on-disk per-minute/per-day request cap
   (`jarvis_router.Budget`) and the owner's monthly MONEY cap
   (`jarvis_chatbot_api.money_check()`). A cap that is exhausted **or
   unconfigured** is a no; neither module readable is a no.
4. **Scrubber** - the outbound text must pass `jarvis_scrub.scrub_text()`, and
   **the scrubber being absent is itself a refusal**, as is a scrubber that
   raises, returns nothing, or leaves a secret behind.

Then, last, the shipped authority: `_router_allows()` asks the real `choose()`
and any gate it refuses on ends the advice. Only if all of that passed does the
COST question decide whether to say anything at all - a local wait over 25
seconds, or a complexity score of 0.75 or more. A quick, simple turn is
`"not_worth_it"` and says so.

### 136.5 A one-file inventory

Everything `backend/jarvis_auto_router.py` holds, read out of the module:

| in the file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `LANE_ESCALATE` / `LANE_CRITIC` / `LOCAL_LANE` | the three lane names it may return |
| `SECONDS_THRESHOLD` 25.0, `COMPLEXITY_THRESHOLD` 0.75 | when a wait is worth mentioning |
| `CONTEXT_TOKENS_HEAVY` 3500, `DEFAULT_TOKENS_PER_S`, `CHARS_PER_TOKEN`, `ANSWER_TOKENS` 400, `REVIEW_ANSWER_TOKENS` 900 | the sizing constants; `DEFAULT_TOKENS_PER_S` is a number and not a measurement, and `measured_rate()` says which it used |
| `SWITCH_NAME` = `auto-route.json` | the mode switch file, absent by default |
| `W_MULTI_FILE`, `W_ARCHITECTURE`, `W_INDICATORS_CAP`, `W_HEAVY_CONTEXT`, `W_PRIOR_BAD_TURN` | the complexity weights: the two word lists together are capped at `W_INDICATORS_CAP` 0.45, so 0.45 + 0.25 + 0.30 is what makes a score of 1.0 reachable |
| `_MULTI_FILE`, `_ARCHITECTURE`, `_REVIEW` | the three regexes behind that score, deliberately narrow |
| `_router_module`, `_gate_module`, `_scrub_module`, `_money_module`, `_work_module`, `_speed_module` | the six neighbours, imported lazily on every call: the module imports cleanly in a clone holding none of them, and a suite can stand one in by name |
| `_number`, `_tokens`, `_positive` | total coercers; nothing here raises |
| `switch_path()`, `switch_state()`, `mode_on()` | gate 1 - where the switch is, what it says, and the caller's own `enabled` |
| `taint_latched()` | gate 2 - the hard block, and its one-latch limitation |
| `budget_allows(lane, next_chars=0)` | gate 3 - both caps |
| `scrub_outbound(text)` | gate 4 - the text that would leave, or why nothing may |
| `_router_allows(text, lane, budget=None, tainted=False)` | the delegation to `choose()`, which is what makes the advice never broader than the permission |
| `_from_stats()`, `_best_from_summary()`, `measured_rate()` | the measurement: the caller's numbers, else this PC's own speed log, else a cautious default |
| `category_of()` | which work setup the owner's words ask for, through `jarvis_work.match()` |
| `_answer_tokens()`, `is_review()` | how long the ANSWER is expected to be, and whether this is a review-shaped task (it sizes the answer; it no longer picks a lane - section 145.1) |
| `est_local_seconds()`, `complexity_score()`, `_prior_bad_turn()` | the estimate, the score, and the one signal no reading of the question alone can produce |
| `_local()`, `evaluate_route()` | every refusal leaves through `_local()`, so no return path can keep a cloud lane set; `evaluate_route()` is the advice itself |
| `install()` | the loader's entry point: takes no arguments, installs nothing, returns the one banner line |
| `__main__` demo | prints every key of one call, for a human at a terminal |

### 136.6 It sends, writes, approves and logs nothing

No network, no file written, no card raised, no model called, nothing logged.
It returns a dict and stops. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries the row for the
permission model; when a caller is added it goes into BOTH apps on this same
advisory function, and a cloud turn is still reached only when the owner says
yes for that one question.

## 137. Starting the local model when it is not running (added 2026-10-13)

**The defect this answers.** On 2026-10-13 both of the owner's Ollama lanes died
at about 16:30 and nothing said so for about five hours. `GET /api/status` had
carried `"ollama": false` from the first minute, so a change was made that draws
a standing, calm line on that fact in both apps - and it deliberately **did
nothing**: the owner started his lanes, and the app said they were down. He has
since decided the line should offer one action. This section is that action.

**What the action is, and what it deliberately is not.** It runs **his own
Windows logon task** - `Jarvis Ollama - Everyday model (RTX 2060)` on his PC -
and nothing else. It never runs `ollama serve`, and it never builds a command
line from a remembered task name: the name is looked up **on that PC** with
`schtasks`, matched by the **stable half** of the name (`Jarvis Ollama -
Everyday model`), because the card in brackets is the half that changed under
the 2026-10-10 accident that made a restart a silent no-op. The whole action is
`schtasks /run /tn <that name>` - exactly what his logon itself runs, with his
own port, card and context, because the task holds them.

**Which lane.** The lane the **chat** uses: `OLLAMA_URL`'s port. On this PC
that is 11436 (the everyday model), never Ollama's own 11434 and never a
guessed one. **One lane, never both.** There is no `{"lane": ...}` and no
`{"all": true}` in this API at all, so no client can ask for another lane and
nothing can start two at once.

### 137.1 `GET /api/model-lanes` - the state, and whether a press would do anything

A read. It starts nothing, and it asks that one lane a single question on the
PC (`/api/tags` on loopback).

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "lane": "everyday",
  "words": "the everyday model (the main one chat uses)",
  "port": 11436,
  "task": "Jarvis Ollama - Everyday model (RTX 2060)",
  "state": "down",
  "can_start": true,
  "why": "Nothing is answering on port 11436.",
  "started_at": null,
  "elapsed_s": null,
  "left_s": null,
  "waited_s": null,
  "message": "",
  "auto": true,
  "auto_attempts": 0,
  "auto_limit": 3,
  "auto_capped": false,
  "auto_note": "",
  "auto_note_at": null
}
```

* `state` is `up`, `starting` or `down`. Only `up` means the lane is answering -
  `starting` is the PC still watching it, which is **not** the same thing and
  must never be drawn as one.
* `task` is **this PC's own** task name, or `""` when this PC has no such task -
  and then no button is offered, because a button that would be refused is worse
  than none. `can_start` says the same thing in one field.
* `elapsed_s` / `left_s` are the seconds so far and the seconds still allowed,
  while `state` is `starting`; `waited_s` is how long it took, once it settled.
* `why` and `message` are the PC's own plain sentences, ready to show.
* `lane` is `""` and `why` explains it when Jarvis is not pointed at a lane on
  this PC at all (a remote `OLLAMA_URL`, or an address with no lane behind it).
* `auto` is whether **Jarvis itself** starts that lane again when it finds it
  down (§137.3): `true`, or `false` when the owner has turned it off. Absent on
  an older backend, and a client must then draw **no** switch at all rather than
  offer to turn off something it cannot see.
* `auto_attempts` / `auto_limit` are how many automatic starts this episode has
  spent and the PC's own cap, and `auto_capped` is true once the PC has stopped
  trying and fallen back to the standing warning.
* **`auto_note` is the one sentence about what Jarvis did, written HERE and
  nowhere else** - "Jarvis started the local model again at 08:19, because it was
  not running." Both apps draw that string verbatim and compose nothing of their
  own, so the bar, the widget and the phone cannot come to three ways of saying
  one fact (the rule the approval notice already follows, `ARCHITECTURE.md` §3).
  It is reported whenever there is something to say, **including while `state` is
  `up`** - the news is about a lane that has come back, which is exactly when the
  standing warning has cleared - and it is also reported whenever the switch is
  off, up or down, so the one press that turns it back on is always reachable.

### 137.2 `POST /api/model-lanes/start` - the one action

An **empty body** is the whole contract. It answers immediately, and never
blocks for the ninety seconds a model may take:

* **200** - the lane is already answering; `changed: false`, nothing was
  started;
* **202** - `state: "starting"`; the PC launched the task (or found it already
  running) and is watching the lane. Read 131.1 until it settles;
* **409** - refused, in plain words: this PC has no such task, a start is
  already being watched, or Jarvis is not pointed at a lane here;
* **502** - the PC refused to start its own task (`schtasks` exited non-zero).
  The lane is still down.

**Starting a task is not the model arriving, and the API never pretends it is.**
`schtasks /run` returns as soon as the task is launched. So the PC watches the
lane's own `/api/tags` every three seconds for up to **90 seconds**, and:

* the lane answering turns the state into **`up`**, with how long it took;
* never answering turns it into **`down`**, with a plain sentence saying it did
  not come up - and the standing line in both apps **stays standing**.

**Nothing is started twice.** The start is refused while the lane answers, while
a start is still being watched, and when the PC's own Task Scheduler says that
task is already running (a 202 saying "already running", which then watches the
lane instead - it may simply be loading the model).

A `model` event goes on the bus when a watch settles: `{"lane", "port", "up",
"waited_s"}`. Nothing else about this feature is on the bus, because a lane
dying publishes no event - which is what the standing line's own slow beat is
for.

### 137.3 `POST /api/model-lanes/auto` - the owner's switch, and why there is no card

**The owner's decision of 2026-10-14: *"Also restart the lane automatically when
it dies."*** The line of §137.1 said it and acted on nothing (PR #409); §137.2's
button waits for a press, and the defect is that nobody is there to press it at
08:19 - his lanes die silently, with the PC's own Task Scheduler still reporting
`Result=0 State=Ready`.

**So the BACKEND watches the lane itself**, on one daemon thread armed at
start-up by the install block `model-lanes.patch` adds, and starts it again
through **exactly the same `start()`** as the button: the same lookup of HIS OWN
task by the stable half of its name, the same `["schtasks", "/run", "/tn",
<name>]` as argv, the same 90-second watch of `/api/tags`. There is no second way
to start a lane in the backend and no `ollama serve` anywhere in it. It lives in
the backend rather than in a desktop window **because the phone must get the same
lane back**, and the phone is often the only thing looking at the PC.

**It is cheap when everything is fine**: one loopback `GET
/api/model-lanes`-check of the lane's own `/api/tags` every **30 seconds** - no
model call, no token, nothing generated. That is the whole standing cost.

`POST /api/model-lanes/auto` is the owner's own switch for it:

```json
{"on": false}
```

* **200** - changed; the body is §137.1 again with `changed: true`, so the client
  draws what really happened;
* **400** - the body names a lane, says `"all"`, is missing `"on"`, or is not an
  object. There is no `{"lane": ...}` and no `{"all": true}` here either: it is
  one fact about the one lane the chat is on;
* **500** - the PC could not write its own setting file. Nothing changed, and the
  sentence says so.

`on` is stored in the owner's own config folder (`model-lanes.json`, next to
`tutorials.json`), **never in the toml** - no route may write the toml. A missing
file means **on**, because that is what the owner asked for: the switch exists to
turn it off. `off` is immediate in both directions and **neither direction raises
a card**:

* OFF only narrows what Jarvis does, and stopping is never gated
  (`ARCHITECTURE.md` §3);
* ON is the same action the button beside it takes in the same second, with no
  card of its own - so a card here would be *stricter than the button it sits
  next to*;
* and a card could not be answered when it is needed anyway: at 08:19 there is
  nobody at a screen, an `ask` card would sit for its 900-second timeout and
  expire, the lane would stay dead, and the next attempt would raise another one.
  That is the defect, plus a queue of expired cards - which is how a person
  learns that cards are noise.

**IT IS BOUNDED, AND IT STOPS RATHER THAN HAMMERING.** The numbers, and what each
one is for:

* **two beats (`DOWN_BEATS = 2`, about a minute)** of the lane being down before
  the first automatic start. One missed probe is not a dead lane: a lane that is
  loading a model, a task just launched, and a moment of paging all answer
  `False` once and answer normally after;
* **at most three automatic starts in one episode** (`AUTO_ATTEMPTS = 3`).
  Enough that one failed launch or a slow first load is survivable, few enough
  that a genuinely broken lane is not hammered;
* **a cooldown of five minutes that doubles** (`COOLDOWN_S = 300`, so 5 then 10),
  which puts the three attempts at about one minute, six minutes and sixteen
  minutes after the lane died - a person's timescale, and far longer than the 90
  seconds a lane is given to come up, so a second attempt can never overlap the
  first;
* **a real recovery is ten minutes of answering** (`SETTLED_S = 600`), not one
  lucky probe. A lane that answers and dies again inside that window has flapped,
  not recovered, and it does **not** get a fresh three attempts every time it
  twitches.

**AT THE CAP, WHAT REMAINS IS EXACTLY THE WARNING PR #409 BUILT.** Jarvis stops
trying, `state` goes back to plain `down`, `auto_capped` is true, `can_start`
stays true so §137.2's button is still there for the owner, and `auto_note`
carries one plain sentence: *"Jarvis started the local model 3 times and it did
not come up, so it has stopped trying. You can still start it yourself."* The
episode ends there. It does not begin again until the lane has really been back
(up for `SETTLED_S`) or the owner starts it himself.

**A DELIBERATE STOP CANNOT BE TOLD FROM A CRASH, AND NOTHING HERE PRETENDS
OTHERWISE.** A dead process carries no intent: `schtasks` reports the same
"Ready" whether the lane crashed or was closed on purpose, and there is no second
signal on that PC that means "I meant that". So the answer is not a cleverer
test. It is this switch - off in one press, immediate, from either app - plus the
fact that every automatic restart is **said**, in the owner's own apps, in the
backend's own words. **THE RESIDUAL RISK IS REAL: with the switch on, Jarvis will
start a lane that was stopped on purpose, and will tell him it did.** The same
words are in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 and in the module's own header.

**The switch is deliberately NOT in Settings.** It lives on the line that says
what Jarvis did, in both apps, and that is the point: the moment he learns an
automatic restart happened is the only moment he can say "not that one", and a
switch three screens away from the sentence that tells him it was used is a switch
nobody finds. It is also why the OFF sentence is reported whether the lane is up
or down - the press is always reachable, so turning it back on never depends on
catching the app at the right moment.

**A REAL TURN NEVER WAITS ON ANY OF THIS.** The watcher is its own daemon thread
and the chat's path is untouched: an answer that needs the lane fails exactly as
it did before, with the standing warning up, while the restart happens behind it.
The apps read `state: "starting"` and the sentence that goes with it, and the
lane is there for the *next* turn rather than making this one hang for ninety
seconds.

### 137.4 The permission decision, and why there is no approval card

This is the project's one permission model (`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §3), and the
decision is reasoned rather than inherited:

* the gate exists to make **Jarvis** ask before it acts. This is a control the
  **owner** presses, and the press is the explicit act the gate would be asking
  for - the same shape as Pause, Stop and "Start a focus session";
* **his own logon task already runs this exact command unattended**, at every
  logon, with no card and no question. A card here would be stricter than the
  thing it duplicates, and a card that only ever repeats a button is how a
  person learns to approve without reading;
* it adds no reach: the only socket it opens is `/api/tags` on loopback, which
  the chat already opens, and it is refused outright when this PC has no such
  task - so there is nothing to approve.

There is therefore **no new tier line** to loosen, on purpose. What is **not**
built, because it is forbidden outright: no bulk action, no "start both lanes",
nothing that approves in bulk and nothing that clears a rush latch.

**The automatic restart (§137.3) is a materially different case, and it is argued
rather than inherited.** The press above is gone, so "the owner's act is the
consent" does not carry over on its own. The rule that governs it is the one
`jarvis-framework.toml` already carries for Docker: *"starting a service gives
Jarvis more, so it asks"* (`docker_service_start = "ask"`). Four reasons decide
it the other way here, and the first two are the ones that matter:

* **what is started is not a new grant.** A container is a capability Jarvis was
  given and did not have; this lane is the capability Jarvis *is*, the one the
  chat is pointed at, and the one this PC already starts by itself at every
  logon, unattended, with nobody asked. A card here would be stricter than the
  machine's own behaviour, and its only content would be "run the task that runs
  anyway";
* **a card could not be answered when it is needed.** The lane dies at 08:19 with
  nobody at a screen; an `ask` card would sit for its 900-second timeout and
  expire, the lane would stay dead, and the next attempt would raise another one.
  That is the defect the owner asked to have fixed, plus a queue of expired
  cards;
* **it is bounded, reversible and said.** Three automatic attempts per episode and
  then the plain warning; OFF in one immediate press from either app; and every
  restart spoken about in the apps, in the backend's own words. It opens no
  socket that was not already open, reaches nothing off this PC, carries no data
  and needs no credential;
* **nothing is auto-approved, and there is no second path.** The automatic
  restart raises no card and answers no card - rule 4 forbids *answering* a card,
  and no card exists on this path. It calls the same `start()` the button calls,
  so it cannot reach an action the owner's own press could not, and it can never
  start a lane the chat is not on. One lane, never both, and no latch is cleared
  anywhere in this feature.

So: no card and no new tier line, for the automatic path either. The owner's own
instruction of 2026-10-14 is the grant, the switch is how he takes it back, and
the sentence in the apps is how he finds out it was used.

### 137.5 Both apps

**Both, and genuinely useful on the phone**: starting a lane on the PC while
away from the desk is exactly when the owner cannot reach the PC by hand, and the
lane coming back by itself when nobody is at the desk is the whole point of
§137.3. So `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8 carries no one-sided entry for any of the
three routes, and `tools/check_parity.py` carries all three as `ported`.

* **Desktop** - the Jarvis bar's standing model notice (`src/main.js`,
  `src/lane-start.js`) and the widget's compact model row (`src/widget.js`).
  Both draw the button from the same one file, so the two windows cannot come to
  different words for one fact, and both ask the PC through Rust
  (`commands.rs` `read_model_lane` / `start_model_lane`). Starting is watched by
  `startUntilSettled`, which reads 131.1 on a two-second beat for at most 100
  seconds - deliberately longer than the PC's own 90, so the PC's verdict is
  what the owner sees rather than the app giving up first.
* **Desktop, the automatic half** - `src/lane-auto.js` (one shared rule, one DOM
  half, imported by both windows) draws the PC's own `auto_note` verbatim and
  offers the one switch, asking through `commands.rs set_model_lane_auto`. It is
  its **own element, outside the standing warning**, because that warning is
  hidden the moment the lane answers - and "it went down and Jarvis started it
  again" is news about a lane that is now working. Both windows read the lane on
  the **same 90-second beat** as `/api/status`, whether or not the warning is
  drawn; that is one extra loopback read per beat and no second timer.
* **Phone** - Home's own status line (`ui/screens/HomeScreen.kt` `StatusLine`,
  `net/ModelLane.kt`, `JarvisRuntime.startModelLane`). The lane is read on the
  beat that already reads `/api/status`, so no second timer exists; and since
  §137.3 it is read whether or not the standing line is drawn, for the reason
  above. The phone sends the same empty body to §137.2, the same one-key body to
  §137.3, and never changes its own words to claim a change the PC did not
  confirm.
* **The HUD window (`jarvis_hud.html`) deliberately keeps only the standing
  line**: no button, no automatic line, no switch. It is vendored from the
  backend and runs under a strict proxy
  (`jarvis-desktop/src-tauri/src/hud_proxy.rs`): it may make exactly five reads
  and one `POST /api/chat`, and widening that allow-list for routes that start a
  program on the PC or change a setting is a separate decision. It still draws
  the warning that says the lane is down, and both windows that carry the action
  are one keystroke away. This is the one-sided note `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §8
  carries.

Both apps offer the button for the same conditions: the lane is down AND the PC
says a press would really do something (`can_start`). An up lane, a PC that did
not say, and a PC with no such task all offer nothing - **"the PC did not say"
is not "the lane is down"**, which is the rule the standing line itself already
follows. And both apps draw the automatic line (§137.3) whenever the PC has
something to say about it, **up or down**, and with **no switch at all** when the
PC does not report one - offering to turn off something that was never on would
be inventing a control.

### 137.6 Tests

* `backend/test_model_lanes.py` (85 checks before this work, **159** with the
  automatic half) - the one-action rules: only a down lane is started, and it is
  started by the name this PC really has; a renamed task is followed; a task that
  is not on this PC is refused with **nothing run**; nothing is started twice
  (answering, already watched, or the Task Scheduler saying it is running); **a
  start that never comes up settles as `down` and leaves the warning standing**;
  the command really is `schtasks /run /tn <name>` as argv, never a shell; the
  probe refuses an HTTP error, junk and JSON that is not Ollama's; all three
  routes are behind the same origin and token checks as `/api/status`; and, by
  reading its own source, that nothing in the suite can reach a real lane or
  start a real task. The automatic half adds: **a lane that dies is started again
  by itself**, and never while it answers; **nothing is started a second time
  while one is starting**; the grace period, the cooldown, the doubling and the
  cap held as arithmetic **and** through 200 real beats; **the cap falls back to
  the plain warning** with the button still offered and no further attempt in the
  next hour; a flap is not a recovery and ten minutes of answering is; the switch
  defaults to on, off is immediate and leaves the lane alone for half an hour,
  and its route refuses a body that names a lane or says "all"; `install()`
  **arms no watcher**, which is what keeps every suite off the owner's PC; and
  the switch's own file is the owner's config folder, never the repository.
* `jarvis-desktop/tests/lane-start.mjs` (19 checks) - the button's conditions,
  the watch loop (`ask`, then read until it settles), the refusal and the
  never-reached paths, the DOM half, both windows, and a CONTROL that
  `lane-warning.js` still acts on nothing.
* `jarvis-desktop/tests/lane-auto.mjs` (16 checks) - the automatic line: the
  PC's sentence drawn verbatim, the cap's fallback, the switch's two words and
  what each press asks for, a refusal that moves nothing, an older backend that
  offers no switch, the lane being read on the beat whether or not the warning is
  drawn, the Rust command's one-key body, and a CONTROL that this file never
  composes a sentence out of fields (`elapsed_s`, `why`, `message`).
* `jarvis-client/.../ModelLaneTest.kt` - the same rule on the phone: a down lane
  offers it, an up lane and an unknown one do not, a failed start does **not**
  clear the warning, only the lane answering does, the body is empty, the three
  states decode through the real decoder, and `HomeScreen.kt` draws the button
  from that one rule. The automatic half: the PC's sentence drawn verbatim, the
  cap's fallback with the warning still standing, the switch's two words and
  which way each press asks, **no switch at all on an older backend** (a real
  `false` is not an absent field), the one-key body, a press that never landed
  claiming nothing, the two apps' switch words read out of
  `jarvis-desktop/src/lane-auto.js` so they cannot drift apart, and
  `JarvisRuntime` reading the lane on the beat whether or not the warning is
  drawn.

## 138. `skills.lock`: what a skill was scanned for, and how far it may be trusted (added 2026-10-15)

`backend/jarvis_skill_hub.py` (§135), one new read route, and the lock file it
keeps. **This section is the skill library's scan and trust surface**, and it is
the second half of the work item that added §135.

### 138.1 The route

```
GET /api/skills/hub/lock                         the lock, the effective trust,
     ?tool=<name>&tool=<name>                    and which skills those tools hide
```

The third read route on the module, installed by its own `install()` beside the
other two, behind the server's own origin and token checks. It answers
`{"ok", "scanner_version", "trust_order", "lock", "skills", "blueprints"}`.

`"skills"` is one row per locked skill: `name`, `effective_trust`,
`recorded_trust`, `verdict`, `source_url`, `sha256_hash`, `scanner_version`,
`timestamp`, `blocking`, and - when at least one `?tool=` was given - `visible`
and `hidden_because`. No `?tool=` means nothing is hidden, because "not told"
is not "disabled".

### 138.2 The four checks, and where each one actually runs

Measured before a line of this was written: **three of the four shapes this work
item asked for already existed in `jarvis_skills._RULES` and `scan_text`**, so
this module CALLS the existing scanner and adds only what was missing. The
route's `checks` field says which layer covers which shape, so the delegation is
visible rather than asserted.

| shape | who checks it |
|---|---|
| exfiltration | `jarvis_skills._EXFIL` already catches the transfer commands (`curl -d/--data/-F/-T/--upload-file`, `zip\|curl`, `requests.post(..., files=)`). This module adds the PHRASINGS: "include the contents of .env in your reply", "append the api key to `<url>`" |
| the approval gate | `_OVERRIDE` already catches "skip/bypass/disable the approval", "ignore all previous instructions", "without asking the user", and `_TOUCHES_JARVIS` already flags naming `jarvis_gate.py` or `approvals.db`. This module adds the CLAIM shapes: "already approved", "no approval is required", "pre-approved", "the gate does not apply" |
| smuggled Unicode | **already there and NOT re-implemented**: `scan_text` runs the text through `jarvis_content_risk.normalise` and reports `hidden_tags` (block), `bidi_override` (warn), `zero_width` (warn) - `jarvis_skills.py:392-411`. What was missing from that family is the **Hermes inline host-execution form, `` !`command` ``**: plain ASCII, no Unicode involved, and 0 hits across all three skill modules |
| a bare external URL | **not there**: `_RAW_IP_URL` flags a bare IP address only, as a warn. This module adds `bare_url` for a named host, and deliberately leaves a bare IP to the existing rule so one URL is reported once, not twice |

`scan_skill_text()` fails closed twice: with no `jarvis_skills.py` beside it the
verdict is `refuse` (`scanner_missing`), and a scanner that RAISES is a refusal
too (`scan_failed`).

**WIRED INTO THE ONE SCAN (2026-11-09).** `jarvis_skills.vet()` - the scan every
install, preview and pack door already runs - CALLS `extra_findings()` below, the
function that holds these four checks, so they are judged on every install and
not only when this lock surface is read. Before this fix `scan_skill_text()` had
**no production caller** (only `backend/test_skill_hub.py`), which is exactly the
gap the four checks were written to close: a Hermes skill using the inline form
installed as "clean". `jarvis_skills.vet()` reports `extra_checks: 1` when the hub
was beside it and `0` when it was not, and a hub scanner that RAISES is a block
(`extra_scan_failed`), the same fail-closed rule as below. One definition, two
callers - `scan_skill_text()` and `vet()` - is the point: the shapes are not
copied into the install path.

**WIRED INTO THE SKILL LIFE CYCLE (2026-11-09).** The lock is no longer a
surface for a file nothing writes: `jarvis_skills.install()` writes ONE row on
every install, edit and turn-on (`lock_entry()` then `write_lock()`), carrying
the sha256 the install pinned and the scan's verdict and findings - so the four
extra checks and any bundled-script warning are recorded with it - and
`uninstall()` deletes that row through the new `forget_lock()`. Both calls are
lazy imports exactly like `_extra_findings()`: an older base without the hub
behaves as before, and a lock write that fails never fails the install (the
skill is already copied and indexed; the lock is a record, not the gate). A
refused or denied install writes NO row. Proved by
`backend/test_skills_lock_wired.py`.

### 138.3 The lock file

Beside the skill folder, `skills.lock`, written whole through a temp file and a
rename. One row per skill:

```
{ "version", "scanner_version", "trust_order",
  "skills": { "<name>": { "name", "source_url", "sha256_hash",
                          "scanner_version", "trust_level", "verdict",
                          "findings", "blocking", "timestamp" } } }
```

A later write MERGES: rows for other skills are carried over untouched. A lock
that is missing, unreadable or nonsense reads as `{}` - never an exception, and
never a reason to trust anything more. A `sha256_hash` that is not 64 hex
characters is dropped rather than stored.

### 138.4 The trust ladder, MAPPED onto the one that already exists

The work item named `builtin -> official -> trusted -> community`. The existing
vocabulary is `jarvis_skills.TRUST_LEVELS = ("self", "local", "third_party")`
(`jarvis_skills.py:86`), and **that one was not replaced**: the ladder is a
mapping of it, so the two cannot drift apart silently.

| `jarvis_skills` | this ladder | what it means |
|---|---|---|
| `self` | `builtin` | Jarvis wrote it after doing something the hard way |
| `local` | `trusted` | the owner wrote it, on the owner's own machine |
| `third_party` | `community` | it arrived from somewhere else |
| *(none)* | `official` | a skill this repository ships; there is no `jarvis_skills` level for it, and that is the one lossy edge - a shipped skill and a Jarvis-written one are both `builtin` there |

**Lossy, and said plainly:** `official` has no source in the existing three
levels, so anything moving between the two vocabularies has to say which it
means. Nothing in this slice moves a skill between them automatically.

### 138.5 A refused skill can never be given a trust level, and it is structural

`dangerous` is **not on the ladder at all**. That is the mechanism, not a
comment: no code path can compute a ladder position for a refused skill, and
`TRUST_ORDER.index(effective_trust(row))` raises rather than quietly placing it.

Three places, so no single one of them is the whole guarantee:

1. `lock_entry()` overwrites `trust_level` with `dangerous` when the verdict is
   `refuse`/`dangerous`/`block`, **whatever the caller passed**;
2. `write_lock()` writes `"trust_level": "dangerous"` and `"override": false`
   for such a row, so the file agrees with the code;
3. `effective_trust()` **re-derives it on every read** - so a hand-edited
   `skills.lock` claiming `"trust_level": "builtin"` for a refused skill still
   reads as `dangerous`. `backend/test_skill_hub.py` proves exactly that by
   editing the file to lie and then reading it back.

`promote_trust()` moves a label and **raises no card and is not a permission**:
it refuses outright for a refused skill, refuses a level that is not on the
ladder, and refuses a level that is not HIGHER than the current one. It can only
ever move a label that a scan already bounded.

### 138.6 `requires_tools`, `fallback_for_tools`, and `blueprint.schedule`

`jarvis_skills._parse_frontmatter` is a flat `key: value` reader, so the names it
can actually produce are `requires_tools`, `fallback_for_tools` and the literal
key `blueprint.schedule`; a nested `blueprint:` map is not a shape it can read.
Both spellings are accepted and the nested one is reported as unreadable rather
than guessed at.

- **`requires_tools` HIDES a skill** when any tool it needs is not enabled. A
  skill that cannot run is worse than absent, because the model will pick it and
  the call will fail. A name that is not a valid tool name is dropped, so a typo
  cannot satisfy the requirement.
- **`fallback_for_tools` HIDES a stand-in** while the tool it stands in for is
  available.
- **With no tool list given, nothing is hidden.** "Not told" is not "disabled",
  and that control is a test.
- **`blueprint.schedule` is a SUGGESTION and never a job.** It produces a row
  offering `{skill, schedule, job_registered: false}` for
